claims.text: Short-range chemical ordering governs the nucleation and stability of protective oxide scales in multiprincipal-element alloys.
The properties and stability of the protective oxide scale control oxidation resistance and long-term material integrity.
Specific thermal-mechanical treatments can introduce controlled levels of short-range order into fine-grained CoCrFeNiMn or FeNiCuAl-based alloys.
Annealing temperature, heating or cooling rate, and cold-working reduction can systematically vary short-range order while composition remains constant.
Short-range order changes grain-boundary character, thereby modifying local thermodynamic and kinetic conditions for selective oxidation and scale adherence.
Greater short-range order fosters preferential segregation and diffusion of Cr or Al toward oxidizing interfaces.
Cr and Al promote formation of thermodynamically stable Cr2O3 and Al2O3 protective scales, respectively.
A dense, continuous, adherent protective scale suppresses oxygen and metal-ion transport, slows further oxidation, and reduces premature scale failure.
Reduced short-range order impedes segregation pathways, delays protective-scale formation, and promotes scale spallation.
Higher-short-range-order samples will establish Cr2O3 or Al2O3 scales faster and exhibit lower mass gain and less spallation than lower-order samples.
A conventional heat treatment can produce a largely random solid-solution baseline with minimized short-range order.
The proposed short-range-order mechanism should apply to homogeneous MPEAs containing Al, Cr, or Mn above approximately 800–900 °C.
Al, Cr, and Mn have important oxide-forming roles in high-temperature MPEAs.
In highly partitioned or intermetallic-rich microstructures, phase-separation effects can overshadow the effect of short-range order on oxidation.
In situ studies and thermodynamic modeling suggest that short-range order affects oxide behavior.
Local chemistry, prior exposure, and interface stresses may complicate the correlation between short-range order and oxidation performance.
Indistinguishable scale thickness, kinetics, and spallation across specimens with genuinely distinct short-range-order states would falsify short-range order as the governing oxidation mechanism.
